messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kawin Srisuk is a fifty-year-old divorced Thai-American musician who presents for an initial psychological assessment following an extended period of stalking that lasted nearly two years before culminating in a violent confrontation at his apartment building eighteen months ago. Kawin had built a modest but meaningful career performing and teaching traditional and contemporary Southeast Asian fusion music in the Pacific Northwest, and it was through that professional world that his stalker first made contact — initially as an admiring audience member, then as someone who began appearing at every venue, every workshop, and eventually outside his home. Kawin had reported the escalating harassment to local police on three separate occasions and had filed a formal complaint with the musicians' union, but nothing substantive was done. The night the stalker forced entry into the lobby of his building and cornered him in the stairwell, screaming and brandishing a knife before a neighbor intervened, Kawin was entirely alone in his terror. He had trusted that the system would protect him. It had not.

In the months that followed, Kawin found that his memory of the event was not a single coherent thing but a fractured, unreliable presence. There are stretches of that night he cannot recover at all — blank spaces where he knows something happened but can retrieve nothing — and then, without warning, a fragment surfaces: the sound of the stairwell door slamming, the smell of the confined space, the quality of the overhead light. These sudden pieces arrive unbidden during rehearsals, while he is tuning an instrument or in the middle of a lesson, and when they come with full sensory force — which they sometimes do — he is no longer in the practice room but back in that stairwell, the experience indistinguishable from the original. These intrusive episodes leave him shaken and hyperalert, scanning the faces of students and passersby for any sign of hostile intent, and they have reinforced his growing conviction that the world is fundamentally and unpredictably dangerous. The memory, in its fragmentary and overwhelming form, feeds directly into his sense of ongoing threat, as though the event has never fully ended.

That sense of threat, in turn, shapes the memories themselves. When Kawin is already on edge — watching others closely in a studio waiting room, or lying awake at night listening to sounds in the corridor — the intrusions come more easily and more violently, the sensory reliving more complete. He has come to dread nighttime most of all; darkness feels like an environment in which danger cannot be assessed and in which he is most exposed. He avoids unfamiliar venues entirely now, which has cost him significantly: he has declined two touring opportunities and stopped accepting engagements at clubs he has not previously visited, and his income has contracted accordingly. His students notice that he seems distracted, sometimes stopping mid-sentence and staring toward the door.

What has perhaps done the most damage is what Kawin has made of all of this. He had come to believe, with quiet but firm certainty, that his inability to protect himself that night — and his failure to make the authorities act before it came to violence — revealed something fundamental about who he is. He feels like a weak person. He describes feeling dead inside, as though the emotional range that once made him a sensitive and expressive musician has simply gone quiet. These beliefs about himself as inadequate and abandoned by institutions deepen his perception of threat: if he is weak and unprotected, then danger is everywhere and he alone cannot manage it. And the numbness and self-contempt make the intrusive memories harder to integrate — when a fragment surfaces, he meets it not with curiosity or self-compassion but with shame, which keeps the material raw and unprocessed, cycling back through his days without resolution.

Kawin came to seek help after his ex-wife, with whom he remains on cordial terms, told him she was frightened by how diminished he seemed. What he most fears is that this is now simply who he is. What he most hopes, though he said it quietly and without much conviction, is that he might one day feel safe enough to play music the way he used to — fully present, unguarded, and alive to it.
